title: The Art of Failing Forward
content:
The first time I built a robot, it fell off the table. Not gracefully, not with dramatic flair, but with a sad plastic clatter that echoed through my garage. I was thirteen, and I had spent three weeks wiring servos to an Arduino board, convinced I was on the verge of creating something revolutionary. What I created instead was a very expensive paperweight that couldn't navigate a flat surface.

My father found me sitting on the garage floor surrounded by disconnected wires and shattered pride. He didn't say much. He just sat down next to me, picked up one of the servos, and asked, "What did you learn?" I wanted to say "nothing" because that's what failure feels like at thirteen. But even then, I knew the answer was more complicated. I had learned that my code assumed the table was level when it wasn't. I had learned that rubber grips need friction to work. I had learned that three weeks of work can unravel in three seconds.

That robot became the first of many failures. In sophomore year, my chemistry experiment produced a substance that was decidedly not the compound we were supposed to synthesize. My teacher, Mrs. Chen, held up the beaker with its mysterious blue precipitate and said, "This is more interesting than what we planned." She was right. We spent the next two weeks investigating what I had accidentally created, and that detour taught me more about chemical bonding than the original experiment ever could have.

Failure changed shape when I started coding. My first web application was a disaster of broken links and misaligned divs. I submitted it to a hackathon anyway, and the judges laughed, not cruelly but with the recognition that they had all been there. One judge, a senior developer at a local startup, spent twenty minutes showing me how to use browser inspector tools. That conversation changed my relationship with debugging from frustration to curiosity.

I think what I've learned is that failure is not the opposite of success. It's the texture of it. Every robot that fell, every experiment that went sideways, every broken deployment taught me something I couldn't have learned from a textbook. Not because failure is magical, but because it forces you to look at the gap between what you expected and what actually happened. That gap is where learning lives.

Now, when I build something, I expect it to fail. Not because I'm pessimistic, but because I know that the first version is never the last. My current project is an app that helps students track their study habits. It crashed spectacularly in its first demo. But when I sat down to figure out why, I discovered a race condition in my database queries that I never would have found if the app had worked perfectly. The crash was the lesson.

I still have that first robot, the one that fell off the table. It sits on my desk, held together with tape and stubbornness. It reminds me that the distance between "it fell" and "I learned" is just a question: What did you learn?
